# Exact projective fiber densities and a nonconvex Ball body

This note formalizes the through-anchor projective change of variables
and disproves convexity of its sampled Ball radial body. The example
uses an actual convex polytope, positive integer fibers, and its true
mixed centroid, which is also a global deepest point. It does not
refute OC. It concerns a Ball body in the continuous slope variables,
not the different ambient angular-volume shadow considered in
`candidate d6a14443e8934b68`.

## 1. Exact positive and negative slope measures

Let `n=1,d>=1`, let `C subset R x R^d` be a convex body, and let
`(j,y) in C intersect (Z x R^d)` be a fixed anchor. Write `K_z=C_z`.
For each positive integer k define

`D_k^+=(K_(j+k)-y)/k`, `D_k^-=(K_(j-k)-y)/k`,

with empty slices interpreted as empty sets. Convexity with the anchor
implies that each of these two families is nested decreasing in k.
For example, if `v in D_l^+` and `0<k<l`, then

`(j+k,y+kv)=(1-k/l)(j,y)+(k/l)(j+l,y+lv) in C`.

Define the finite sampled slope densities

`f_+(v)=sum_(k>=1) k^d 1_(D_k^+)(v)`,
`f_-(v)=sum_(k>=1) k^d 1_(D_k^-)(v)`.                       (1)

The sums are finite because C is bounded. Both are integrable
nonnegative densities, with total masses equal to their respective
strict-side mixed volumes. The exact Jacobian in each original fiber
is `dx=k^d dv`; no sum over lattice fibers is replaced by a continuous
integral over the integer projection.

Every through-anchor closed ambient halfspace has the form

`H={a(z-j)+u dot(x-y)>=0}`, `(a,u)!=(0,0)`.

Using `x=y+kv` on BOTH strict sides gives

`vol_MI(S intersect H)
 =vol_d(K_j intersect {u dot(x-y)>=0})
   +integral_(u dot v>=-a) f_+(v)dv
   +integral_(u dot v>= a) f_-(v)dv`.                       (2)

Thus its oblique integer coefficient becomes an ordinary threshold
in the slope variables, with the indicated opposite signs. Formula
(2) also covers `u=0`: the central fiber is then entirely on the
closed boundary, and the appropriate strict integer side contributes
in full. Boundary fibers are not dropped.

## 2. A convex reciprocal ray function does not smooth the sampling

For real slope v set

`R_+(v)=sup{t>=0:(j+t,y+t v) in C}`,
`R_-(v)=sup{t>=0:(j-t,y+t v) in C}`.

Each ray intersection is the closed interval from zero to its finite
endpoint, possibly just zero. Consequently, pointwise for the closed
slice indicators,

`f_+(v)=sum_(k=1)^(floor R_+(v)) k^d`,
`f_-(v)=sum_(k=1)^(floor R_-(v)) k^d`.                      (3)

At an integer ray endpoint the final slice is included. Slices of
zero d-volume have no effect on the Lebesgue integrals in (2), though
the displayed canonical pointwise density retains their closed traces.

Let `K=C-(j,y)`, a compact convex set containing zero, and use its
possibly extended-valued Minkowski gauge

`p_K(w)=inf{lambda>=0:w in lambda K}`.

Then

`1/R_+(v)=p_K(1,v)`, `1/R_-(v)=p_K(-1,v)`,                  (4)

with `1/0=+infinity`. The gauge is convex: if two vectors belong
to positive dilates of K, their convex combination belongs to the
corresponding convex combination of those dilates, by convexity of
K and `0 in K`; taking infima proves the inequality. Therefore the
two functions in (4) are extended-valued convex functions of v.
No assumption that the anchor lies in the ambient interior is needed.

The sampled densities in (3) nevertheless have jumps. In particular,
neither reciprocal-gauge convexity nor nestedness supplies the
log-concavity hypothesis of the ordinary Ball-body theorem.

## 3. Ball-body convention and its exact radial formula

For a nonnegative density f on `R^d`, use the radial construction

`rho_f(e)^d=d integral_0^infinity t^(d-1) f(t e)dt`,
`B_f={s e:|e|=1, 0<=s<=rho_f(e)}`.                         (5)

Its gauge, when the radial integral is positive, is

`g_f(v)=[d integral_0^infinity t^(d-1)f(t v)dt]^(-1/d)`.

This formula is for any nonzero, not necessarily unit, direction v.
Indeed rescaling the ray parameter contributes exactly `|v|^(-d)`.
Some conventions divide f by `f(0)`; that only dilates this body by
one common positive factor and does not affect convexity.

If all the relevant `D_k` contain zero, the sampled density (1) gives

`rho_(f_+)(e)^d=sum_k k^d rho_(D_k^+)(e)^d
                    =sum_k rho_(K_(j+k)-y)(e)^d`.           (6)

This is a radial d-power sum. Convexity of the original fibers and
their projective nestedness do not in general make it convex, as
the next explicit body shows.

## 4. Actual five-fiber polytope and deepest anchor

In two continuous dimensions let

`Q=[-1,1]^2`, `D={(x_1,x_2):|x_1|+|x_2|<=1}`,
`C=conv( ({-1,1} x Q) union ({-2,2} x D) )`.

This is a full-dimensional compact convex polytope in `R^3`.
Its integer projection is `{-2,-1,0,1,2}` and its exact integer
fibers, in that order, are

`D,Q,Q,Q,D`.                                               (7)

The extreme fibers at `z=+-2` are D by extremality of their base.
Every generator has continuous coordinate in Q, so every fiber is
contained in Q; the slab `[-1,1] x Q` is contained in C and makes
the other three displayed fibers equal to Q. This proves (7)
without assuming a fiber description not induced by C.

The source mass is `2+4+4+4+2=16`. It is centrally symmetric, and
each fiber has continuous centroid zero, so its true mixed centroid
is the anchor `(j,y)=(0,0)`. This anchor is in the interior of its
positive-area source fiber. It is a global deepest point of depth
exactly one half. A nonvertical through-zero plane has zero source
boundary mass, and inversion exchanges its two halfspaces, giving
mass eight on each side. A vertical through-zero halfspace has
mass ten, including the whole central fiber. Any halfspace containing
zero contains a parallel through-zero halfspace. Conversely, at any
candidate point, two opposite nonvertical closed halfspaces through
it have total mass sixteen because their boundary has zero source
measure, so one has mass at most eight. This proves the exact
global depth assertion with all boundary cases retained.

## 5. Exact failure of convexity in the slope Ball body

On the positive integer side, (1) becomes

`f_+=1_Q+4 1_(D/2)`.                                      (8)

These are nested full-dimensional convex sets containing zero in
their interiors. Their total density integral is `4+4(1/2)=6`,
the exact mass of the positive source fibers.

For the nonunit ray `v_s=(1,s)`, `0<=s<=1`, the square persists
to ray parameter one and `D/2` persists to `1/[2(1+s)]`.
Consequently (5) gives

`g_(f_+)(1,s)=[1+1/(1+s)^2]^(-1/2)
                  =(1+s)/sqrt((1+s)^2+1)`.                 (9)

This is strictly concave on the displayed affine line segment:

`d^2/ds^2 g_(f_+)(1,s)
       =-3(1+s)/[((1+s)^2+1)^(5/2)]<0`.

An exact three-point violation of gauge convexity is

`g(1,1/2)=3/sqrt(13)
       > (1/sqrt(2)+2/sqrt(5))/2
       = [g(1,0)+g(1,1)]/2`.                              (10)

For a rational certificate of the strict sign, multiply (10) by two
and square its positive sides. It reduces to
`191/130>4/sqrt(10)`, and a second positive squaring reduces this
to the integer inequality `36481>27040`.

The body in (5) contains zero in its interior, has continuous positive
radial function here, and its gauge is (9). The gauge of a convex
body containing zero is convex: convex combinations of points in its
positive dilates give the triangle inequality after normalizing the
coefficients. Thus (10) proves that this Ball body is not convex.
Equivalently, set `p=(1,0)`, `q=(1,1)`. The points `p/g(p)` and
`q/g(q)` lie on its radial boundary, but their convex combination
with weights `g(p)/(g(p)+g(q))` and `g(q)/(g(p)+g(q))` equals
`(p+q)/(g(p)+g(q))`, whose gauge is greater than one by (10).

The violation is also strict on an open sector by (9), so changing
the density on isolated sampling boundaries does not repair it.
Every source fiber in this example has positive area; there is no
lower-dimensional-density version issue. The anchor is already the
true centroid and a global deepest point. The failed inference is
therefore specifically that nested sampled projective densities
automatically possess convex Ball radial bodies.
